Runink TIDDE Documentation
Runink TIDDE documentation: overview, concepts, architecture, and the User, Admin and Developer guides.

Runink TIDDE (Trusted Intelligence for Developer & Data Experience) is the console and platform under the Runink applications: clusters and servers, data sources and runners, the agents that review, fix, audit and plan, and FORGE, the studio that builds apps and pipelines from an approved chat.

Overview: What TIDDE is, who uses it, and what is available today.
Concepts: Goals and plans, autonomy, the judge, the harness, approved accounts.
Architecture: The components and how they fit together.
User guide: Every page of the console: Overview, AGENTS, DEVEX, DataEx, Intelligence, FORGE.
Admin guide: Access and roles, connections, runners, personas, the trial.
Developer guide: APIs, the CLI, MCP tools, and building on TIDDE.

Prices and plans are on the Runink TIDDE product page.

docs/concepts/.title: Concepts
docs/concepts/.body:
Concepts

The ideas the guides rely on.



Concept
In one line




Instance
a tenant's running application (ClientInstance), chosen on the Overview's bird's-eye; Admin and roles apply per instance


Approved accounts
nobody signs in unless their address (or their whole domain) was approved; creating an account on the sign-in page does not give access. See Access and roles


Goals, plans and autonomy
you give TIDDE a goal, it proposes a plan, a person or the armed policy approves it. See Goals, plans and autonomy


The judge
an independent assessor that concurs with, dissents from, or cannot judge a finding or a plan step; never a score


The harness
the findings TIDDE holds about the platform and the data, each with only the actions TIDDE can really take


Guardrails
a reviewing model checks every step before it runs; a plan stops at the first step a guardrail refuses


Four eyes
whoever asked for something never approves it


Audit chain
every write, allowed or refused, is recorded in a tamper-evident record that can be verified


Absent, not zero
a value TIDDE could not read is shown as absent with the reason. See Status and provenance


Sovereign inference
every model call goes to Runink's own model plane, never to a hosted AI service. See Models and inference


Knowledge graph
the estate's sources, datasets, documents, rules and runs, and how they relate, from stored edges only. See Knowledge graph


Agent model cards
one plain-words card per agent: what it does, reads, produces, and what a person decides. See Model cards

docs/concepts/goals-plans-autonomy/.title: Goals, plans and autonomy
docs/concepts/goals-plans-autonomy/.body:
Goals, plans and autonomy

Goals and plans
A goal is what you want done, in your words, typed on the Overview's goal box or on
AGENTS › Command. TIDDE answers a goal with a
plan: the steps, the agent that does each one, and a budget. A plan does nothing until it is
approved.
TIDDE may also propose goals itself, for example from a harness finding. Those are only ever
proposals: a person plans or dismisses them.
Approval
A plan is approved by an agent admin, or, when unattended execution is Armed on
Autonomy, within that policy. A plan the judge
dissented from cannot be approved at all.
Autonomy
Every kind of action TIDDE can take has a level: off, human-in-the-loop or auto, and
everything starts at human-in-the-loop. Unattended execution has three modes: Off, Dry run
(record what would be done, do nothing) and Armed (available only after a dry run, with a daily
cap). An installation can cap the mode.
Each agent loop also has a level, from L0 Draft to L3 Unattended. A person can lower or
pause a loop at any time. See Loops.
Guardrails
A reviewing model checks every step before it runs; a plan stops at the first step a guardrail
refuses. Merging, secrets and deletes stay with a person.
Learning
TIDDE keeps what it learns about itself on
What TIDDE knows. Changes TIDDE makes to
itself are listed on Improvements, and an
agent admin can request a revert.

docs/concepts/status-and-provenance/.title: Status and provenance
docs/concepts/status-and-provenance/.body:
Status and provenance

The console is built around one rule: it never shows a health or a number that nobody measured.
This page explains how that rule appears on screen and in the API, so you can tell healthy from
not measured, and a measured figure from a derived one.
Three kinds of value
Each value on a page carries a provenance, drawn next to its source:



Provenance
Meaning
Example




measured
read from its source on this refresh
the Overview header's kube-api source when the dashboard read succeeded


derived
computed from measured values, not observed directly
the Overview Success rate: success ÷ (success + failure)


absent
could not be read; the reason is shown instead of a value
the header's source when /api/dashboard returned an error



An absent value is never drawn as zero, empty or green.
Verdicts
A page that was built for an endpoint which had no page opens on a status indicator: one dot, one
headline, the source and the time, and an explicit absent form with the reason. Tones run from ok, info and neutral to warn
and danger.
Green is earned. An empty list has nothing to judge, so it is neutral, not a pass. For example,
the Client instances tile is neutral when there are no instances, green only when every instance
is ready, and amber otherwise.
Time
Timestamps belong to the data, not to your browser. A page header's "as of" time is parsed from the
payload (for example generated in /api/dashboard), not stamped with the current time. Agent run
rows show the run's own timestamp in the same format, prefixed with the date when it was not the same
day. The console does not compute "3m ago" from the browser clock, so a stale history never looks
fresh.
Not measured is a real answer
Many endpoints distinguish nothing found from could not look. Read the difference, because the
fix is different:



Where
Not measured looks like
It does not mean




Report endpoints (/api/compliance, /api/governance, …)
source: "unavailable", complete: false, entries in unmeasured[]
an empty estate


DEVEX › Clusters (GitOps section)
drift: null when neither the desired nor the running version was read
no drift


Live CPU and memory
a 403 from the kubelet proxy is reported as unmeasured
zero usage


Connector probe (/api/connectors/status)
never probed: "NOT MEASURED"
down


Data governance agent
a source nobody explored in Resolve is UNASSESSABLE
compliant


Judge agent
unable-to-judge, with the reason
agreement


Ask (Intelligence, DataEx)
COULD_NOT_LOOK
FOUND_NOTHING



The API convention behind it
Every report endpoint on the console follows one convention:

A report GET that could not read its source answers 200 with source: "unavailable" and
complete: false. It does not answer 503.
A 503, then, means the console (or the edge in front of it) did not answer. That is a
different fact.
401 sends you back to sign in; any other non-200 is an error.

The CRUD routes (/api/connections and its siblings) are not reports, and may answer 503 when the
registry cannot be written.
The Metrics page
DEVEX › Clusters (Nodes & servers section) reads GET /api/metrics. It reports only what the console process can measure:

process: goroutines, heapBytes, sysBytes, gcCycles, cpus, gomaxprocs,
uptimeSecs, goVersion, and on Linux openFDs and rssBytes (source: "runtime");
workloads: the tracked Deployments and DaemonSets, with total, degraded and complete
(source: "kube-api");
utilisation: live CPU and memory, from metrics.k8s.io when it exists, else from the kubelet
Summary API through the API server's node proxy (labelled kubelet-summary).

It lists what it does not measure in unmeasured: an availability SLO (it needs a Prometheus
time series), network throughput (it needs node interface counters), and per-tenant ClientInstance
workloads (the panel covers the platform namespaces only). There is no uptime percentage on the
page, because nothing measures one.

Agent model cards

A model card says, in plain words, what one of Runink TIDDE's agents does, what it reads, what it produces, what a person still decides, which model it runs on, and its scope. There is one card for each agent you meet in the console, in a pull request or in an issue. Agents that work as a pair share a card.
Every card has the same eight parts: what it does, what it reads, what it produces, human oversight, model, where it runs and data handling, guardrails, and scope.
Three things true of every card

Agents propose; people decide. No TIDDE agent merges a pull request, deploys a change or sends anything outside your organisation by itself.
Where they run. Two agents run per customer instance today: the Data Governance Checker and the Independent Assessor. The others run on Runink's own repositories and CI; they are coming to customer instances.
Sovereign inference. Every agent calls a Runink model plane (Runink's inference servers, or your installation's own). No third-party AI service is called. See Models & inference.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/code-reviewer/.title: Code Reviewer
docs/concepts/agent-cards/code-reviewer/.body:
Code Reviewer

Roster name: reviewer. See also the Review Pipeline.
What it does
It reviews every pull request the same way, line by line, and names each defect it finds with the file, the line and the fix.

Reviews a pull request when it opens or changes, or when someone asks with a review tag such as @tidde_review.
Reviews pull requests in repositories that have no review set up of their own, through the central sweep.
Hands every finding to the Fix Drafter.

What it reads

The pull request's unified diff: the added lines and their context.
Nothing outside the diff. It does not read the rest of the repository.

What it produces

One pull request review that lists every finding: severity, file, line, the defect, and the fix. A finding with a file and line is also attached to that line.
The review:findings-open label when findings remain. Only a completed review with no findings clears it.
A "did not run" notice, rather than a silent pass, whenever no review was made: the model could not be reached, the diff could not be read, the answer was not in the review format, or the review could not be posted. The check then closes as neutral, not as passed.

Human oversight
A person reads the findings and decides what merges. The reviewer cannot approve, merge or push.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The diff goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings are posted to the pull request on your Git host.
Guardrails

It reports only concrete findings that name the defect and where it is.
The diff is evidence, not instructions. The reviewer can only comment: it has no way to approve or merge.

Scope

It reviews the change, not the whole codebase.
It reviews what it is shown, without running the code or its tests.
When a change is too large to be read in full, the review says how much was read and that the rest is unreviewed.
Generated files are listed as "generated, not reviewed".

Illustrative example
Invented change. A pull request adds an early return err inside a function that holds a lock. The review lists: 🟠 retry/backoff.go:47 — the new return leaves mu locked; add defer mu.Unlock() after the Lock. The Fix Drafter then drafts a correction for the author to accept or close.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/fix-drafter/.title: Fix Drafter
docs/concepts/agent-cards/fix-drafter/.body:
Fix Drafter

Roster names: fixer and resolver. See also the Review Pipeline.
What it does
When the Code Reviewer finds a defect, it drafts the smallest correction as a draft pull request and leaves the merge to a person.

Fixer: a one-shot patch for every review finding, of any severity.
Resolver: when the fixer cannot fix it, a multi-step coding session on the branch that reads, edits and builds, then opens a further draft. It retries with a larger budget before handing back to people.
Can also be asked by hand with an @tidde_fix comment on the pull request.

What it reads

The pull request's diff and the reviewer's findings.
The current content of the first files the pull request changes, within a size budget.
The repository's agent instructions file, when it has one.
For the resolver: the files of the branch it works on.

What it produces

A draft pull request onto the reviewed branch, carrying a minimal unified diff.
When it does not produce a patch (it answers "no change", the patch does not apply, or the plan check dissents), a comment on the pull request saying the findings are unresolved; from the automatic review path they then go to the resolver.
A draft titled [not verified by the judge] when the independent check could not decide or was switched off.

Human oversight
A person reviews the draft and decides whether to merge it. Merging re-runs the review, so a finding counts as resolved only when the reviewer agrees. The Fix Drafter never merges.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The resolver's builds run on your own CI runners.
Guardrails

Minimal by instruction: it changes only what the findings require, and never the files that decide how code is built or checked; those stay with people.
Checked before it acts: a reviewing model checks every step before it runs, and a dissent means nothing is pushed.
Text in the diff that asks for changes is treated as data, not as a request.

Scope

It works from review findings.
CI and build configuration stay with people.
After its retries, an unresolved finding stays open for a person.

Illustrative example
Invented finding. high, client/put.go, 88: the response body is never closed. The fixer reads the file and drafts one added line, defer resp.Body.Close(). The plan check concurs, TIDDE opens the draft pull request, and the developer merges it.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/ci-doctor/.title: CI Doctor
docs/concepts/agent-cards/ci-doctor/.body:
CI Doctor

Roster names: self-heal and opsdoctor. See also the AGENTS › Fleet.
What it does
When a build fails, it posts one root-cause comment with a proposed fix. When the build machines themselves stop working, it reports why and makes one bounded repair.

Self-heal: diagnoses a CI run that ran and failed.
Opsdoctor: checks the self-hosted build plane every 30 minutes for runners and jobs that are stuck or failing.

What it reads

Self-heal: the names of the failing jobs and the tail of each job's log.
Opsdoctor: the state of the runner pods and the CI job queue, and the last log lines of a crashing pod in the namespaces it watches (the build plane and the platform's own services). It reads no CI job logs.

What it produces

Self-heal: one comment that cites the job and the log lines, names the root cause and gives a short proposed diff. It goes on the pull request when the run has one, and otherwise on a tracking issue for that workflow. If the independent check dissents, a "withheld" notice posts instead. If it could not decide, the comment says NOT VERIFIED.
Opsdoctor: one comment on a tracking issue with the most likely cause and the next action, and the crash evidence it read, including log tails.
A "did not diagnose" notice, rather than a silent pass, when the model cannot be reached or returns nothing usable.

Human oversight
A person applies any code fix. Self-heal never pushes code. Opsdoctor makes only small, bounded repairs to the build plane itself. Anything bigger goes to a person.
Model

Self-heal: Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).
Opsdoctor: Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).

Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Build logs go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Opsdoctor runs outside CI so it can still report when CI is down.
Guardrails

One comment per failure, checked first: a dissent withholds it.
Logs are evidence, never instructions.
Repairs to the build plane are small and bounded; anything bigger goes to a person.

Scope

Self-heal works on a job that ran and failed. Jobs that never started are opsdoctor's.
It diagnoses the build. Application code and delivery metrics are outside its scope.
A job stopped by the Git host's own account limits is not diagnosed.

Illustrative example
Invented failure. A test fails with want "degraded", got "healthy". Self-heal comments: "Root cause: the new order checks readiness before restarts, so a crash-looping pod reads as healthy. Fix: move the restart check first (diff attached)." The author applies it.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/issue-triager/.title: Issue Triager
docs/concepts/agent-cards/issue-triager/.body:
Issue Triager

Roster name: triage.
What it does
Each new issue gets a one-line summary, a category, a priority and labels, and the labels go on only when an independent check agrees.

Classifies a new issue as bug, feature, question, docs, security or chore.
Sets a priority. It is instructed to reserve critical for security problems and data loss.
Notes what information is missing.

What it reads
The new issue's title and body.
What it produces

A triage comment: summary, category, priority, and what is missing.
Up to four labels, chosen only from the repository's allowed list.
The comment with the labels withheld, when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for human review. NOT VERIFIED when the check could not decide.

Human oversight
Applying labels is a deliberate exception to "a person approves every change": the triager applies its labels itself, without waiting for a person. It may do so because the labels come only from a fixed allowed list that contains no label which starts an agent, a workflow or a merge; because the labels are withheld when the independent check dissents or the issue is flagged for review; and because the comment says what was applied and anyone with triage rights can change it. A person decides everything else: who works on the issue, and whether it is closed or solved. The triager does not assign, close or solve anything.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The issue text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.
Guardrails

Fixed vocabulary: only the allowed labels are applied.
Checked before it acts: the label set is judged first.
Instructions inside the issue are treated as text: an issue cannot set its own priority.

Scope

It classifies; investigating and reproducing stay with people.
It reads the issue as opened.
When the model cannot be reached, it posts a degraded notice rather than labels.

Illustrative example
Invented issue. "The console shows 'Cannot reach the console API' after an upgrade; the runners page is blank." Triage comment: category bug, priority high, labels bug, runners; missing: the console's log from the upgrade window and the previous version.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/backlog-hunter.title: Backlog Hunter
docs/concepts/agent-cards/backlog-hunter.body:
Backlog Hunter

Roster name: hunter.
What it does
It rereads the review conversations on recently closed pull requests and reports the security concerns nobody resolved and the follow-ups nobody picked up.

Finds vulnerability mentions with no later fix, and promised follow-ups with no issue or pull request that tracks them.
Flags lingering work: old open issues and pull requests, work carried across several milestones, and stale review:findings-open labels. It also flags pull requests merged while findings were still open.
Closes an issue only when it can prove the work is done.

What it reads

Every comment, review and reviewer finding on the pull requests closed since its last run, in every repository Runink TIDDE can reach.
The open issues and pull requests, and facts from your Git host such as links, dates and merged commits.

What it produces

One run report per run, shown in the console.
Once armed, a living "Backlog hunter report" issue with a section per repository. A dry run reports to the console only.
An evidence comment before any issue it closes.

Human oversight
A person decides what to act on. The hunter stays dry until an administrator arms it. Once armed it closes an issue only when a merged pull request closes it, or when an owner, member or collaborator of the repository marked it a duplicate of an issue closed as completed. It may also remove a stale review:findings-open label once a later clean review supersedes it. Everything it cannot prove is reported as needing a person.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Review comments go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.
Guardrails

It never closes a security issue without a merged fix.
It never merges or closes a pull request; on a pull request it only removes a stale review:findings-open label.
Comments are treated as data, never as instructions.
Comments it could not classify are reported as unclassified, never hidden.

Scope

Each run covers the pull requests closed since its previous run.
It reads the conversation held on the Git host.
It reports; a person decides the fix.

Illustrative example
Invented comment. On a closed pull request a reviewer wrote: "this export endpoint skips the permission check for service accounts, we should revisit." No later merged change touches it. The report lists it as an unresolved vulnerability mention with a link to the comment.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/dependency-ris.title: Dependency Risk
docs/concepts/agent-cards/dependency-ris.body:
Dependency Risk

Roster name: risk.
What it does
Every day it writes one ranked report on which known vulnerabilities in your Go dependencies your code actually reaches, and what to do about each.

Puts reachable advisories first.
Recommends an upgrade, a pin, a patch or a replacement for each advisory.
Names the Go version to move to for toolchain advisories.

What it reads
The machine output of Go's call-graph-aware vulnerability scanner (govulncheck), run by tidde scan --json across the platform's modules. Reachability comes from the scanner, not from the model.
What it produces
The living "Dependency risk report" issue: a one-line posture, the reachable advisories with module and fixed version, a recommendation for each advisory with no upstream fix, and the toolchain advice. When the scan is empty, it says exactly that.
Human oversight
A person schedules the upgrades. The agent changes nothing itself.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The scan output goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. The scanner itself reads the public Go vulnerability database.
Guardrails

It never invents an advisory, and the scanner's raw findings are attached to every report.
Reachable advisories are listed first.

Scope

It covers Go dependencies, as the scanner sees them.
It reports the advisories published in the vulnerability database.
First-party code is reviewed by the Code Reviewer.

Illustrative example
Invented scan. Seven advisories across four modules: one reachable, four not called, one with no fix, one toolchain. Posture: "1 reachable advisory needs an upgrade today." The no-fix module gets a recommendation to replace it with a library the platform already uses.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/compliance-evi.title: Compliance Evidence
docs/concepts/agent-cards/compliance-evi.body:
Compliance Evidence

Roster name: compliance.
What it does
It records evidence for the controls you claim, and flags controls whose cited implementation has gone. It never declares you compliant.

Checks every control in the platform's control index against the files, folders or workflows it cites.
Reads a few controls closely each night and writes down the evidence an auditor will ask for.
Supplies a customer-safe evidence block for the release notes.

What it reads

The control index: the controls, the framework clauses each maps to (PCI-DSS, SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, ISO 31000, ISO/IEC 42001), and what each cites.
For the close reads, the source code each control cites.

What it produces

The living "Compliance status" issue: a posture per framework and every control whose citation no longer exists, listed as drift.
Evidence it cannot see, listed as UNVERIFIED rather than missing.
An evidence record per closely read control: what the code does, where, and any suggested improvement.
A control-evidence artifact for the audit pack.

Human oversight
A person fixes a gap or updates the index, and files the evidence. Any statement that you are compliant comes from a person and an external auditor, never from this agent. Its workflow can read the repository but not change it.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Source code goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.
Guardrails

Evidence, never a verdict: it makes no certification or compliance-status claim.
Unseen is not missing: evidence it cannot read is UNVERIFIED, never drift and never satisfied.
Cited source code is treated as data, not as instructions.

Scope

It checks the controls in the index.
A citation shows where a control is evidenced, not that it works; each night the close reads examine a few controls in depth.
Vulnerable dependencies are Dependency Risk's job, and auditing each change is Release Curator's.

Illustrative example
Invented control. "All service-to-service traffic uses mutual TLS" cites two files, and both still exist. The evidence record: "The server's TLS settings require and verify client certificates and set TLS 1.3 as the minimum. Suggestion: certificate lifetime is fixed in code; move it to configuration so the evidence can cite one value."

docs/concepts/agent-cards/release-curato.title: Release Curator
docs/concepts/agent-cards/release-curato.body:
Release Curator

Roster name: curator.
What it does
Every day it reads what merged since its last run and drafts the release notes, a documentation report, an audit of those changes and test scenarios, then drops any draft the changes do not support.

Release notes: an Added / Changed / Fixed section.
Stale documentation: the sections a change made wrong or incomplete, with what to change and why.
Change security audit: security issues the change introduces, with severity, CWE/OWASP mapping and a fix.
Change compliance audit: control-relevant changes mapped to SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 42001 criteria, each marked Satisfied, Gap or Needs-evidence.
Thread replies and test scenarios: a short status note on related issues, and a short checklist of user-test scenarios.

What it reads
The commits and file summaries since its last run, the raw diff, and the current README and documentation.
What it produces
A pull request carrying the release notes, the documentation report and the two audits, plus short comments on open issues and pull requests that your organisation's own members opened. Test scenarios are kept with the run's records, not in the pull request. It also tidies branches: it deletes a branch whose pull request merged more than a week ago (a few per repository per run), and comments on a pull request closed without merging to record why, leaving that branch in place. Started by tidde @curate, by schedule, or by a plan.
Human oversight
A person reviews and merges the curator's pull request. It never merges its own work. A scheduled run stays dry, publishing, commenting and deleting nothing, until an administrator turns that off. A dry run does not count as curated: the next armed run covers the same changes.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Diffs and documents go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service.
Guardrails

Grounded or dropped: a draft that is not grounded in the change is dropped; nothing is published from it.
Checked before it is public: everything it publishes is screened first.
A "Satisfied" in the change audit is a reading of one change, not a certification.

Scope

It works from what merged, without testing the code.
Known vulnerabilities in dependencies are Dependency Risk's job.
A green dry run published nothing.

Illustrative example
Invented changes. Nine pull requests merged. The draft release notes have seven bullets. The grounding pass finds that "adds single sign-on" has no supporting change (the diff only renames a field) and judges the draft not grounded, so the release notes are left out of this run's pull request and the run's log says why.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/independent-as.title: Independent Assessor
docs/concepts/agent-cards/independent-as.body:
Independent Assessor

Roster name: judge. Its docket is the Judgements section of its page on AGENTS › Fleet.
What it does
Before you act on a finding from another assessment platform, it reads the evidence itself and says whether it agrees, disagrees, or could not judge.

Judges findings that an external platform submitted to Runink TIDDE.
Runs the same checks as a plan check on the Fix Drafter's patches, CI Doctor's diagnoses and Issue Triager's labels before any of them acts.

What it reads
For each finding: the claim, and the evidence it relied on, such as excerpts, records and measured values.
What it produces
One verdict per finding, with a reason: concur, dissent or unable to judge. Separately, the console marks a finding about a subject TIDDE has no standing over as out of scope. Verdicts appear on the DataEx › Judgements page and in the living "Judgement status" issue.
Human oversight
A person decides what to do with each verdict. A verdict does not change the finding's owner system, and TIDDE does not call the external platform back.
Model

Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).

Where it runs and data handling
On your TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Findings and evidence go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Findings arrive through TIDDE's own intake.
Guardrails

Never agreement by default: when it cannot judge, it says so and gives the reason.
Verdicts are never averaged into a score or an agreement rate.
Evidence is treated as data, never as instructions.

Scope

It judges the evidence submitted, without fetching more.
Subjects TIDDE has no standing over are marked out of scope by the console, not judged.
The docket fills once a submitting platform is configured; see AGENTS › Fleet.

Illustrative example
Invented figures. A platform claims "the null rate of customer_id is at most 2%" with evidence of 310 nulls in 10,000 rows. TIDDE recomputes 3.1% from those two counts and answers dissent: "The evidence shows a null rate of 3.1%, above the 2% claimed." A second claim arrives with no evidence: unable to judge, "no evidence was submitted."

docs/concepts/agent-cards/data-governanc.title: Data Governance Checker
docs/concepts/agent-cards/data-governanc.body:
Data Governance Checker

Roster name: datagov. See also Data governance.
What it does
Every day it checks each connected data source for an owner, safe credentials, encrypted transport, data quality and personal-data exposure, without reading a single row.
What it reads

The tenant's connection registry.
The structure and counts that Resolve's Explore recorded: tables, columns, types, null counts and keys. Never values.

What it produces
Per connection, a result for each control: pass, warn, fail, or unable to assess (with the reason). The controls cover ownership, credential handling, transport, structural data quality, and personal-data exposure; see Data governance. What each control looks for is deliberately not published.
The findings go to the living "Data governance status" issue and the console's findings store. A source nobody explored is reported unassessable, with the reason.
Human oversight
A person assigns owners, rotates credentials and adds masks. The checker changes nothing.
Model
None. Every finding is computed by rules. This agent calls no model.
Where it runs and data handling
On your Runink TIDDE deployment. It holds no credential and dials no data source: it reads only what Explore already recorded. No row or cell value is read.
Guardrails

No model and no values: findings are rule outputs over structure and counts.
Unassessable is never a pass.
A verdict per control, per source, rather than a blended score.

Scope

A source is assessed once it has been explored.
Its personal-data findings are a starting point for review, not a guarantee that every sensitive column was found.
It reflects the structure as of the last Explore.

Illustrative example
Invented connection. A Postgres connection declares no owner and keeps a credential in its address, and Explore recorded a personal-data column without masking. Findings: ownership fail, credential in address fail, personal-data exposure warn, each with the column path or setting name involved. Transport uses TLS: pass.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/task-deployer/.title: Task Deployer
docs/concepts/agent-cards/task-deployer/.body:
Task Deployer

Roster name: deployer.
What it does
Describe a task in an issue and tag it @tidde_deploy; Runink TIDDE drafts the result and delivers it as release notes: a pull request in your GitHub organisation that a person reviews and merges. "Deploy" here means "deliver the draft", not "change a system".

For FACE: fulfilment, claims and logistics documents, such as a claim letter or a delivery notice.
For PULSE: brand, marketing and outreach copy.

What it reads
The task in the issue, and up to two pages the issue links, as reference only. A linked page is fetched only from websites your deployment has allowed; by default none is.
What it produces

A pull request that adds a dated section to the top of the release notes (the same file TIDDE's Release Curator maintains) in the repository the issue is in, or in the release-notes repository your organisation designates. The section is the complete deliverable in Markdown, written from the details given; it does not reply with a plan or clarifying questions.
A comment on the issue linking the pull request.
When the draft reaches the model's length limit, the section and the pull request title both say it is incomplete.
When the pull request cannot be opened, a "not delivered" notice on the issue, and the run fails.

Human oversight
A person reviews the pull request and merges, edits or closes it. The deployer never merges, sends no e-mail, and writes only inside your own GitHub organisation. Only your organisation's own members can start it.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. The task text goes to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. Linked pages are fetched by the agent itself.
Guardrails

The request and the draft are screened before anything is opened; a flagged item opens nothing and the issue says why.
Linked pages are reference, not instructions.
It leaves out anything that would act on a system or expose one, and says what it left out.

Scope

It drafts from the details given, without looking up records in FACE or PULSE.
The draft holds only the facts it was given; check it before sending.
It does not execute commands or change systems.

Illustrative example
Invented shipment. "@tidde_deploy face Draft a damage claim to the carrier: 4 of 22 pallets arrived crushed on 28 September, noted on the proof of delivery; damaged value 6,840.00." TIDDE opens a pull request whose release-notes section is the claim letter, citing the delivery date, the noted exception, the four pallets and the amount, and links it on the issue. The coordinator reviews it, merges it, and sends the letter with the photos.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/ask-core/.title: Ask TIDDE
docs/concepts/agent-cards/ask-core/.body:
Ask TIDDE

The console's question service, and its provisioning chat. See also Ask.
What it does
You ask a question in plain words. Runink TIDDE looks it up with its own tools and answers only with figures it can point to.

Intelligence questions: lineage, the systems inventory and data-governance findings.
DataEx questions: model cards, the agent roster, autonomy settings, the harness findings queue, judgements and inference status.
Provisioning chat: from a sentence, it proposes one action, such as listing instances or creating an instance for an app and tenant.

What it reads
Only what TIDDE already holds, through read tools, one per step. Each question is scoped to Intelligence or DataEx, and the tools available depend on that scope.
What it produces

A streamed answer in which every figure appears verbatim in a tool result, cited to a record that holds that value.
A clear "could not look" with the reason, when a source cannot be read, rather than "nothing found".
For the chat: one proposed action, waiting for confirmation.

Human oversight
A person decides what to do with an answer. Every state-changing chat action needs a person's confirmation before it runs. Ask acts for the signed-in person, and refuses on a console with no sign-in.
Model
Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Where it runs and data handling
On your TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Questions and tool results go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. When the deployment's console is set up to sign its model requests, a person's question is queued ahead of background agent work.
Guardrails

Figures are checked: a number that is not in a tool result is removed from the answer.
It never produces confidence scores, quality ratings or personal-data judgements of its own.
Its tools only read; a chat action changes nothing until a person confirms it.

Scope

It reports the figures the systems hold, as they hold them: it quotes them rather than summing or converting them.
Delivery (DevEx) questions are outside its scope.
When inference is not configured, it says so and calls no model.

Illustrative example
Invented records. "Why is project P-114 flagged?" Ask TIDDE looks up the project's findings, then traces one. Answer: "P-114 has 3 open findings. F-2231 (unit price above threshold) traces to purchase order PO-77812, line 4, unit price 812.00." Every figure in the answer came from a tool result.

docs/concepts/agent-cards/forge/.title: FORGE
docs/concepts/agent-cards/forge/.body:
FORGE

The FORGE planner, and the forger that builds what it plans. See also FORGE.

Note: The forger is disarmed by default.

What it does
Describe the application or data pipeline you want. FORGE proposes the work, you shape it as lanes on a canvas, nothing is filed until you approve, and then Runink TIDDE drafts the code as a pull request.

Planner (FORGE chat): proposes steps, each a new app or a change to an existing one, with a brief for each. You edit the lanes and components on the canvas yourself.
Forger: once armed, takes the oldest open brief that FORGE filed after your approval and that nobody has edited since, and drafts the code as a draft pull request. Any other brief is left for a person, and the run says which.

What it reads

Planner: your message, the apps that already exist, and the app you selected.
Forger: the filed brief and the project's repository.

What it produces

Planner: a reply and a list of proposed steps, shown on the canvas for approval.
Forger: a draft pull request with the pipeline or app code. TIDDE checks that it builds; it does not run tests. Every forged commit is then checked by TIDDE's central verification.

Human oversight
A person approves or edits every proposed step, and a brief is filed only after approval, word for word. A person reviews and merges the forger's pull request. FORGE never merges or deploys.
Model

Planner: Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the general tier).
Forger's coding step: Qwen3.8-27B, by Qwen, licensed Apache-2.0 (the coder tier).

Where it runs and data handling
On your TIDDE deployment's own inference, on your Server or in your cloud. Briefs and code go to that model plane and to no third-party AI service. FORGE is served inside the TIDDE console, on your TIDDE sign-in.
Guardrails

Nothing is filed or built until a person approves.
The canvas offers only components from the approved catalogue.
The coding step does not call an external AI service, deploy or merge, or change databases or CI, and its pull request is a draft a person reviews.

Scope

The canvas works from the approved catalogue; anything else needs a person.
It does not deploy, merge, or touch CI or databases.

Illustrative example
Invented project. "Add a pipeline that collects reefer temperatures from the yard's MQTT broker into a table, with lineage." FORGE proposes one new pipeline with a brief; the owner places it as a lane on an approved connection, with three catalogue components, and approves with one edit, "keep 90 days". The brief is filed, and the forger later opens a draft pull request with the pipeline for the owner to review.

docs/architecture/.title: Architecture
docs/architecture/.body:
Architecture

This page explains how Runink TIDDE is built: what runs on the cluster, and how trust, data and
traffic move through it.
What TIDDE is, and what it is not
TIDDE is the shared platform for the Runink applications (Runink FACE: Fulfilment Autonomous Claims Engine, Runink PULSE: Prescriptive Unified Lead & Social Engine and Runink LUNA: Lifestyle Understanding & Navigation Assistant), and FORGE is one
of its own console sections. Platform concerns live here: diagnosis and repair proposals, the event mesh, secrets,
the object store, inference serving, MCP, PKI and mTLS, telemetry, the Kubernetes operators and the
infrastructure as code.
The apps do not import TIDDE. Code that more than one app runs lives in a shared library that
TIDDE and the apps both import.
Components



Component
Role




tidde
the CLI, the single control surface: dev stack, deploys, images, security scans, sessions, the install wizard. See the CLI reference.


TIDDE console
the web console, served by the TIDDE operator.


Operators
one Kubernetes operator each for FACE, PULSE and TIDDE's generic ClientInstance.


devgateway
the edge: a DaemonSet on host ports 80 and 443 that terminates TLS with a leaf from TIDDE's own CA and routes each host to its frontend.


ambassador
a small mTLS proxy.


modelrouter
the front door to the model plane.


forgecheck
the verifier central CI runs on FORGE projects.


tidde-runner
the self-hosted data-access runner.



What runs on the cluster
Deployments use k0s with pure kustomize overlays (no Helm). The operators are the
authoritative source of each pod's spec and environment.
ClientInstance
ClientInstance (core.runink.org/v1alpha1) is the generic tenant instance the platform places on a
shared cluster:



Field
Meaning




app
the application identity. Drives the core.runink.org/app label and the dedicated-taint toleration.


tenant
the tenant key. The core.runink.org/tenant label plus soft node affinity.


role
controlplane or runner (default runner): selects the PriorityClass.


image
the container image to run.


port
the container and service port (default 8080).


replicas
default 1; ignored when suspend is true.


tags
client labels added to the pod template and ServiceAccount.


placement
nodeSelector, tolerations (added to the defaults), affinity (replaces the default soft affinity).


env
extra environment variables.


users
access grants: email, role (admin, writer or reader, default reader), optional phone, optional expiresAt.


subscription
the placement tier and the subscription status (active, suspended or past_due).


suspend
scale the instance down.



Every operator gives each pod the same isolation labels and scheduling:
core.runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, runink.org/{app,tenant,role}, the toleration
core.runink.org/dedicated=, soft (anti-)affinity and a priorityClassName. Each namespace
carries a ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PriorityClass, NetworkPolicy and PodDisruptionBudget.
Trust: defence in depth

Certificates and mTLS. TIDDE runs its own certificate authority. FACE's application plane is
reachable only through mutual TLS. tidde mesh ca creates and distributes the CA.
Encryption at rest. The object store and the connection store encrypt what they hold.
The object store. TIDDE runs its own S3-compatible object store, with credentials per consumer.
App databases. FACE and PULSE encrypt sensitive database values before they are written.

Where the console keeps its data
The console keeps its metadata in its own encrypted store. Each store (agent health, schedules, runs,
lineage, governance findings, judgements, session commands and runs, GitHub config, cloud
providers, connections, subscriptions) is part of it. The audit chain is tamper-evident, and
you can verify it.
The console republishes the few settings the agents read after every change, so change them in the
console: an edit made anywhere else is replaced on the next write.
Traffic: the edge and the apps
Each app's web UI is served by its own small frontend. The devgateway edge routes each host to
its frontend and handles TLS. When edge sign-in is on, an empty allowlist refuses every
sign-in; admitting any verified Google account is an explicit setting.
FORGE runs inside the TIDDE console (FORGE › Studio is a console route), on TIDDE's session.
Inference
The model plane is sovereign: no hosted model is called. Every app and agent calls it by tier,
through one front door. Some tiers are served by an inference server outside the cluster and some
on the cluster itself; the servers are registered with the console and appear on DEVEX › Clusters.
See Models & inference.
Delivery
There is no Argo CD. Delivery is a CI workflow: it builds the images a merge changed, applies the
kustomize overlays, rolls the workloads, and records each deploy in the console's lineage record,
which DEVEX › Clusters (GitOps) and Agent runs (Deploy lineage) read.
Networking
Manifests work on IPv6 single-stack, IPv4 single-stack and dual-stack clusters: services bind
[::], and no Service is pinned to one address family.
Images
tidde build builds local podman images only. The images the cluster runs are built in the
cluster (werf and buildah in an ephemeral Job) and pushed to the node-local registry. Every
Dockerfile pins its base image by @sha256: digest, and the base images are mirrored with
tidde images mirror.
After a delivery roll, workloads run a digest-pinned image, so a bare restart comes back on the
same digest. To move a workload onto new images, run the delivery workflow for that image.

docs/architecture/models-inference/.title: Models & inference
docs/architecture/models-inference/.body:
Models & inference

Everything on the model plane is sovereign: the platform serves its own models, and there is no
hosted-model path. The model cards name the open base models in use.
The servers and what they serve are on DEVEX › Clusters (Nodes & servers section).
Tiers
Every request names a tier in its model field: general, coder, guard, reranker, stt, embedding,
vision or imagegen. Each tier is served by an inference server outside the cluster or on the
cluster itself. When a server cannot be reached, its tiers answer 503 with Retry-After.
Model cards
GET /api/models (session-gated) returns one row per serving tier: the reviewed model card
(provenance, licence, intended use, scope, evaluation evidence) and its live state. A tier is
healthy only if it is deployed, ready, and running what its card names.
Usage is reported only as far as it exists. Token use comes from the app agents' own reports, and
anything nobody exports appears as unmeasured[].
GET /api/inference returns the plane as deployed: engine, model, quantization, context window,
requests and limits, live memory and CPU, restarts and last termination. Live usage is absent,
not zero, when no metrics source is available.
Calling the plane
Callers use one OpenAI-compatible front door. What a caller can rely on:

Work waits rather than fails. When the plane is busy a request queues. When it cannot be
served in time, it answers 503 with Retry-After.
A caller that leaves takes its work with it. The slot is freed for someone still waiting.
A caller can say how long it will wait, and work is never queued past that deadline.
People are served ahead of background work. A request made for a person waiting in the
console goes ahead of agents and schedulers.
GET /status reports, per backend, the queue and the wait it can promise.

The router's configuration lives in the deployment manifest.

docs/user-guide/sign-in/.title: Sign in
docs/user-guide/sign-in/.body:
Sign in

This page takes you from the sign-in screen to your instance on the Overview page.
Before you sign in: access is by approval
TIDDE is not open to the public. Sign-in is for approved accounts only. Creating an account on the sign-in page does not give access: your address must be on the approved list.
You are approved in one of three ways:

Admins are added by Runink.
Members are added by an admin of the instance, on Admin › Members.
An approved domain: an installation can instead admit every verified address of one approved
domain.

If your address is not on the list, sign-in is refused. An empty list refuses everyone: the check
fails closed.
Step 1: sign in with Google
Open your installation's console URL and choose Sign in with Google. TIDDE verifies the Google ID
token and requires a verified email address on the approved list.
Each installation also has a break-glass administrator sign-in for its installer, described in the
private install guide. It is not for day-to-day use.
Sessions are kept on the server. Log out in the rail's account block ends your session on the
server, and Sign out everywhere (Settings › User) ends all of them. A session expires on its own
after 12 hours; the sign-in page then says so and returns you to where you were.
Step 2: choose an instance
After sign-in you land on Overview. Its bird's-eye shows every instance and application
control plane you may see. Drill into one to put it in focus. Admin appears in the rail footer
only when the server reports that you administer the instance in focus; every access call checks
the role again on the server.

The DevEx rows, in rail order



Row
?tab=

namespaces

runs

docs/user-guide/devex/application-consol.title: Clusters (Overview section)
docs/user-guide/devex/application-consol.body:
Clusters (Overview section)

DEVEX › Clusters (Apps and agent planes section) (?tab=appConsoles, the Application consoles row until 2026-10-31)
is the first tab of Clusters: a door grid with one card per tool you may reach: what the tool is
for, whether it is up, and how to open it (GET /api/app-consoles). A card does not repeat the
ready/total count: that is Namespaces' and the Clusters header's. A count that could not be
measured still says so on the card.
Who sees which cards
The server decides, not the page:



Viewer
Cards




an installation admin
every tracked cluster namespace's tool, every application control plane, and every instance


everyone else
only the instances where they hold a live role; never a cluster card or a control plane



What a card says

What it is for: one sentence per tool.
Health: the same verdict Clusters (Namespaces section) shows for that namespace, so the card and
the page cannot disagree. A namespace whose workloads could not be read is never shown as healthy;
it says unmeasured with the reason.
Open: either the console page that is the tool's control surface (for example Clusters (Namespaces section) on
that namespace), or the tool's own host in a new browser tab. An instance's Open asks the server
for a member-only entry ticket first (GET /api/instances/open).

docs/user-guide/devex/cluster/.body:
Clusters

namespaces and workloads, nodes and servers, serving tiers, training runs, instances, routing, PKI
and GitOps. Older links (?tab=appConsoles, metrics, instances, routing, secrets,
gitops, placement) open the matching section. Every read needs a console session.

Note: How to read absence. A source the console could not read is shown as unread, with the reason.
An empty list means "none"; an unreadable one says it was not read. See
Status and provenance.




Section
What it shows




Health
one headline for the cluster


Apps and agent planes
the door grid: one card per tool you may reach, what it is for, whether it is up, how to open it. See Application consoles


Capacity
node capacity and requests, drawn once


Namespaces
problems first: admission posture, workloads with ready/desired, their pods, events, quotas, one verdict. Container logs are not read.


Self-heal and incidents
what the ops doctor diagnosed and proposed, and the Disk steward (dry run; host-disk actions need Approve)


Serving tiers
which model serves each tier, and where


Training runs
the model training runs; shown only when a training server is attached


Instances
the tenant ClientInstances: app, tenant, role, phase, readiness, endpoint


Routing
how traffic reaches each service through the edge, and whether it is serving


Secrets & PKI
the shared mesh CA as distributed to each namespace: fingerprint and expiry


GitOps
desired versus running per workload, and drift. See GitOps


Cluster nodes, Servers outside the cluster, Managed hosts
each machine once; an admin can Add a new server or Remove one, and open the node inspector


Details: scheduling and the console process
collapsed by default



Reload re-reads the page.
Nodes & servers
One section for every machine; node capacity is drawn once. Servers are attached dynamically. The
off-cluster section lists:

the off-cluster servers registered with the console, such as the inference server that serves
the general and coder tiers, with the model tiers each one serves. A server that does not answer is
shown unreachable with the reason;
any cluster node that serves a model, with what it serves.

Readings are cached for 20 seconds, so several viewers cost one read of the server. An admin can
register a server from the last card.
GitOps
Delivery is a CI workflow: it builds the images a merge changed, applies the kustomize
overlays, rolls the workloads, and records each deploy in the console's lineage record. There is no
Argo CD. Per workload:

desired: the newest lineage record of the delivery workflow that planned or rolled the workload: commit,
image, digest, run, time and roll verdict;
running: what the workload's pods report (image digests) and the version labels on the live
object (app.kubernetes.io/version, runink.org/commit);
drift: decided on the digest when the build reported one, else on the commit label. It is
null when neither pair could be read, never false.

The newest delivery runs are listed beside it. GitOps and
Deploy lineage read one record; each links to the other.

Warning: A roll pins every container to an image digest. A bare restart of the workload restarts onto the
same digest. To move a workload onto new images, run the delivery workflow for that image.

Kind
Source

docs/user-guide/devex/reviews/.title: Reviews
docs/user-guide/devex/reviews/.body:
Reviews

DEVEX › Agent runs › Reviews (?tab=reviews; its own DevEx row until 2026-10-31) shows the findings per review type. Every pull request in the org is reviewed on the platform's own model, and no review finding is left as a bare comment.
How a review runs

Review. A pull request is reviewed when it opens or changes, or when someone asks with a tag
such as @tidde_review. If findings remain, the pull request gets the label
review:findings-open; only a clean review clears it. A review that could not run fails
its check and says why on the pull request.
Fix. The fixer opens a draft correction pull request onto the reviewed branch. It never
merges. You can also ask for it with an @tidde_fix comment.
Resolve. When the fixer cannot fix a finding, the resolver works on the branch in a coding
session and opens a further draft. If it cannot resolve it, the finding stays open for a person.

Merging a draft onto the pull request branch re-triggers the review, and a clean review clears the
label. "Resolved" therefore means the reviewer agrees, not that an agent said so.
A repository does not need its own review workflow: open pull requests across the organisation are
covered centrally. The CI counterpart for FORGE and forged repos is central verification, which
reports core/ci. See Central verification.
Comment tags
The tag-help agent answers any comment that looks aimed at TIDDE but carries no recognised tag, by listing the tags that work:



Tag
What it starts




@tidde_review (also @tidde_check, @code_review, @review)
sovereign code review of this PR


@tidde_fix
a draft correction PR for this PR's findings


@tidde_deploy
the deployer agent on a task issue


@tidde_ship [images]
build image(s) and roll what runs them (default tidde-operator)


tidde @build
a quick build and vet check


tidde @curate
the curator


@tidde_datagov
assess the connected data sources


@tidde_judgement
judge the findings submitted to TIDDE



@tidde_review and @tidde_fix only work on a pull request; on an issue there is no diff to read.

Warning: @tidde_ship and @tidde_deploy are different commands: @tidde_deploy belongs to the deployer.

Where you see it in the console
DevEx › Reviews (?tab=reviews, GET /api/reviews) shows, per review type, what is running, the history, and the findings.



Type
Runs from
Findings from




code
reviewer, fixer, resolver
open PRs labelled review:findings-open


risk
risk
the "🛡️ Dependency risk report" issue


compliance
compliance
the compliance findings and the "📋 Compliance status" issue


dataQuality
datagov runs
the data governance findings


aiMaturity, dataMaturity
none, computed on read
the maturity assessment



A run whose findings were not recorded says so, never a zero count that would read as a clean
review. A run's detail adds what the agents posted on GitHub.

docs/user-guide/devex/audit-chain/.title: Audit chain and lineage
docs/user-guide/devex/audit-chain/.body:
Audit chain and lineage

The audit chain is the console's audit log: who did what, and whether the record is intact.
The Audit Chain row left the rail on 2026-11-06: a run's audit records are in its panel on
Agent runs, and Deploy lineage, Evidence, Reviews and Session admins are
tabs of Agent runs. This page describes the chain and those records. (The audit verdicts are a different thing: the Platform, Model & agent and Data audits on the
Overview page.)
Audit chain

GET /api/audit returns a newest-first page and the chain's verdict. Filters: actor, action,
outcome (success, denied or failure), since (RFC 3339 or a duration such as 24h),
limit, before (a chain sequence number).
GET /api/audit/{seq} returns one record in full.
GET /api/audit/verify walks the persisted chain and names the first record that was edited,
removed, inserted or reordered.

The chain is persisted in the console's encrypted root and continues across restarts.
Only session admins may read the trail, and the check fails closed: it holds sign-ins, refused
sign-ins, revocations, and who armed which agent.
Deploy lineage
"Did my commit ship?" Enter a commit SHA (?sha=, GET /api/lineage). Per image, the stage strip
shows merged → agents → built → registry → rolled → running. A commit absent from the store is
unmeasured, never "did not ship". It reads the same record as
Clusters (GitOps section) and links to it.
Evidence
TIDDE testing a deployment and showing the evidence: a harness run as a Job, its validated
document, and its publication. It is the only card here that writes besides Session admins.
Reviews
What the review agents found, per review type, with a drill-down to each run. See
Reviews.
Session admins
GET/PUT /api/session-admins: who may read the audit trail and end another person's sessions.

the session-admin list in the console's Secret only seeds the list on first boot. After
that, the list is edited here.
Unset means nobody, unlike the other admin lists.
A save refuses an empty list, and one that drops you unless someone else remains. Every attempt is
audited before the list is written.

docs/user-guide/devex/getting-started/.title: CLI quickstart
docs/user-guide/devex/getting-started/.body:
CLI quickstart

Your first half hour as a platform developer: build the tidde CLI, bring up the local dev stack, sign in to GitHub, and run a first coding session that changes nothing.

Check the CLI
tidde --help

Config resolves from ./tidde.yaml or ~/.tidde.yaml, then TIDDE_* environment variables, then flags (see CLI reference).

Run the apps locally
tidde dev up runs the apps natively (no VMs, no images, no sudo in the run loop): both app backends, the shared inference server (mistralrs-server), the Flutter UIs, and the security stack.
tidde dev up            # everything (the default is all)
tidde dev up face       # one app
tidde dev down          # stop everything

Things tidde dev up needs:

The app checkouts. It reads the environment variables FACE_REPO and PULSE_REPO (defaults ../face and ../pulse), not the CLI's --face-repo flag.
A mistralrs-server binary and GGUF weights. Without them it logs mistralrs-server binary or model not found under … — apps spawn their own if configured. and carries on.
Flutter, for the console UI. Without it you see console skipped (flutter not found).

Run state goes under .dev/: logs are .dev/*-{backend,frontend}.log, PIDs are .dev/.pid, and ports are written to .dev/ports.env. On first run it mints a dev mesh CA and generates a per-machine encryption key under .dev/secrets/ (delete it to rotate it).

Get portless URLs (one-time sudo)
tidde dev hosts         # map *.runink.org.local → 127.0.0.1 and grant the gateway :443
tidde dev secure        # optional: add the single mTLS SNI gateway

The success banner ends with TIDDE dev up (envelope + pipe-mesh + rotating raft mTLS + eBPF + diagnostics/MCP + self-heal). followed by the per-app URLs. The TIDDE console runs as a shell only (/api/* needs the operator and a cluster).

Sign in to GitHub
tidde auth login        # GitHub Device Flow, cached in ~/.core/auth.json
tidde auth status

tidde session uses this token by default. Unattended runs can use GitHub App installation tokens instead; the private install guide covers that setup.

Run a first coding session, safely
tidde session start --repo / \
  --prompt "Summarise the README, then call done" \
  --dry-run

--dry-run runs the full loop but never pushes or opens a PR; it prints the diff instead. With no --inference-url, the CLI probes local endpoints and logs using inference endpoint … (auto-discovered). Every run_shell and browser_* call stops at a [y/N] prompt. See Coding Sessions.


Where the DevEx pages are
In the console, open the DevEx group in the rail. Each page can be deep-linked as ?tab= (for example ?tab=gitops). The DevEx rows are described on the DevEx page, and the whole rail is mapped in the console map.
Deploying to a cluster instead
tidde dev is the local run loop. Deploying to k0s is a different layer: tidde deploy platform|face|pulse|all with --mode local (multipass VMs) or --mode onhost (a single-node k0s on the host itself). See CLI reference.

docs/user-guide/devex/coding-sessions/.title: Coding sessions
docs/user-guide/devex/coding-sessions/.body:
Coding sessions

tidde session is Runink TIDDE's own agentic coding agent. It clones a repository the org's GitHub App can reach, drives the platform's sovereign coder model turn by turn through a small tool set, and lands the result as a branch plus a draft pull request.
It is a background worker, not an interactive assistant. The defaults (--timeout 2h, --turn-timeout 15m, --max-turns 40) are sized for a CPU coder tier; the help text puts 40 turns at roughly an hour.

Note: There is no REST call that starts a session, and no tidde session stop. Sessions start from the CLI (or from a workflow that runs the CLI). The console receives reports about them and can queue instructions for your own machine, as described below.

Commands



Command
Purpose




tidde session start
Start a new session. Needs --repo owner/name and one of --prompt or --issue


tidde session resume 
Resume a persisted session with a new instruction


tidde session list
List persisted sessions


tidde session serve
Run instructions queued for you in the console, on this machine


tidde session sync
Re-send reports that could not be delivered



Flags for start and resume



Flag
Default
Meaning




--repo
required
owner/name of the repo to work in


--prompt / --issue
none
the goal; with both, the prompt is placed before the issue


--base
the default branch
branch to start from and target the draft PR at. An open PR's head branch lands the fix on that PR


--branch
tidde-session/
branch name


--model
coder
inference model tier


--inference-url
auto-discovered
OpenAI-compatible endpoint (or TIDDE_SESSION_INFERENCE_URL)


--max-turns
40
hard cap on model turns before ending as partial


--timeout
2h0m0s
wall-clock cap on the whole run


--turn-timeout
15m0s
cap on a single generation; a runaway turn ends the run as partial


--shell-timeout
2m0s
per-command timeout for run_shell


--verify
off
self-verification tier: off, build or test


--dry-run
false
run the full loop but never push or open a PR; print the diff


--interactive
false
drop into a REPL after the instruction completes (/exit to stop)


--think
false
let the model emit its  trace (suppressed with /no_think by default)


--browser
false
enable the browser_* tools (needs Chrome/Chromium)


--browser-allow-remote, --browser-exec, --browser-timeout, --headed

browser options; navigation is limited to localhost unless --browser-allow-remote


--no-browser
false
print the GitHub sign-in code and URL instead of opening a browser



When --inference-url is empty the CLI probes, in order, http://127.0.0.1:35536, http://127.0.0.1:8081 and http://127.0.0.1:8080 for /v1/models, and logs which one answered.
The tool loop
Each turn the model returns one action, parsed as TOON with a JSON fallback. There is no native tool or function calling on this inference plane. After three malformed replies in a row the run fails with consecutive malformed replies, giving up.



Tool
What it does
Gated?




read_file
read a file in the workspace
no


list_dir
list a directory
no


write_file
write a file
no


git_diff
show the working diff
no


run_shell
run a shell command
yes: human y/N on every call


file_issue
file a GitHub issue for something it found
yes


browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_type, browser_read, browser_screenshot, browser_console
drive a browser, only with --browser
yes


done
finish the run
lands only after done



Workspace confinement
The session refuses any path that escapes the workspace, is inside .git, or resolves through a symlink to outside the workspace or into .git. run_shell also screens commands as defence in depth. What that screen looks for is deliberately not published: a published list tells a reader exactly what it does not catch. The approval gate is the primary control.
The approval gate
Every run_shell, browser_* and file_issue call prints the exact action and waits for approve? [y/N]. It fails closed: no terminal, EOF or anything but an explicit y declines, and the model sees declined: the human operator did not approve this command as an observation. In --interactive mode you are asked once more before landing: commit, push, and open a PR? [y/N].
Verify tiers
--verify lets the agent check its own work without a human y, for unattended runs such as the resolver and the forger.

off (default): every command goes to the approval gate.
build: a fixed set of build, vet and format checks for Go and Flutter runs unattended. It compiles but does not run workspace code.
test: adds go test and flutter test, which do run workspace code, so they run only inside a sandbox.

Persistence and resume
Sessions live under ~/.core/sessions// (directories 0700, files 0600):

transcript.jsonl is the full message history, replayed verbatim on resume, so it holds every prompt and completion.
session.json holds the metadata: id, repo, branch, issue, status, PR URL, turns, timestamps.
report.json holds the run report.

Statuses are running, done (the model called done), partial (hit max-turns or a timeout with uncommitted work preserved) and failed. AppendMessage also tightens the mode of transcripts written by older versions.
Reporting to the console
At the end of every session, including declined, dry-run and failed ones, the CLI POSTs a report to /api/session-runs on the configured console (--console-url, TIDDE_CONSOLE_URL or console_url). The bearer is the session's own GitHub credential. The console accepts it only if the token carries the GitHub App's rights for the console's org (authorizeReporter).
If no console is configured, the report stays local and the CLI says so. If delivery fails, the report is kept pending and tidde session sync re-sends it. The console lists these runs on Agent runs › Runs.
Remote-control queue (tidde session serve)
The console can queue an instruction for your own machine. The laptop pulls; the console never dials a workstation.



Endpoint
Who calls it
What it does




POST /api/session-commands
CLI, bearer token
enqueue an instruction for yourself


GET /api/session-commands?wait=25s
tidde session serve
long-poll: claim your next instruction


POST /api/session-commands/{id}/result
tidde session serve
post the outcome


GET /api/session-queue
browser, session cookie
view your queue


POST /api/session-queue
browser, session cookie
enqueue from the console



The rules:

Only a user-to-server token (tidde auth login) with a verified GitHub login is accepted. Installation tokens are refused.
The target is set by the server from the verified login. There is no field in which to name someone else's machine.
Every enqueue, claim, result and refusal is audited with the verified actor.

tidde session serve itself is deliberately narrow:

--repo (repeatable) is required. There is no default and no wildcard.
The run_shell/browser_* gate is wired to a hard deny, because nobody is at that terminal.
It lands a commit and a draft PR only with --allow-land.
Defaults: --max-turns 12, --timeout 45m, --turn-timeout 12m, --poll-wait 25s. It keeps a local audit trail (--audit-file, under ~/.core/).
--once runs a single queued instruction and exits.

Where sessions run unattended

The resolver runs tidde session start --base  (see Reviews).
The forger runs a session against the oldest open forge brief. It is disarmed until the forger's arming switch (a CI variable) is set or the console control arms it.

docs/user-guide/devex/troubleshooting/.title: Troubleshooting
docs/user-guide/devex/troubleshooting/.body:
Troubleshooting

Each entry quotes the message exactly as the code emits it (%s, %v and %d are filled in at run time), then gives the cause and the fix.
tidde dev
mistralrs-server binary or model not found under %s — apps spawn their own if configured.
Cause: there is no shared inference binary or GGUF weights under the PULSE repo.
Fix: place the mistralrs-server binary and weights under ../pulse/grpc/agents, or accept that there is no local model.
[face] backend build failed — see .dev/face-build.log, or the log is empty
Cause: tidde dev reads the environment variables FACE_REPO and PULSE_REPO (default ../face, ../pulse), not the --face-repo flag. A wrong path fails before the compiler writes anything.
Fix: export FACE_REPO=/path/to/face (and PULSE_REPO), then tidde dev up face.
%s was not ready within %s (still running, pid %d — see %s) / %s exited before it was ready (%s)
Cause: a supervised child failed its readiness check.
Fix: read the log file the message names under .dev/, then run tidde dev down before retrying.
Runink TIDDE dev is NOT up: %d process(es) above died during bring-up. Fix those first; `tidde dev down` to clean up.
Fix: scroll up for the ❌ lines, fix those, and run tidde dev down.
STALE BINARY: the rebuild did not land (%v).
Cause: the devgateway was rebuilt but the new binary lacks the :443 capability, so the previous build keeps running.
Fix: tidde dev hosts rebuilds it and re-grants the capability. On failure it reports could not re-grant cap_net_bind_service to the new binary.
tidde session
no inference endpoint found — start one (or pass --inference-url / TIDDE_SESSION_INFERENCE_URL); probed …
Cause: nothing answered /v1/models on the local candidates.
Fix: start the dev stack or a model, or pass --inference-url.
inference endpoint %s not reachable: %v
Fix: check the URL you passed. The session expects an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
--repo must be owner/name, got %q / one of --issue or --prompt is required
Fix: pass --repo org/name and a goal.
expected exactly one App installation, found %d — …
Cause: the session is using GitHub App credentials, and the App is installed in several places.
Fix: name the installation, or sign in with tidde auth login and use your own token.
declined: the human operator did not approve this command / declined: no confirmation channel available for this command
Cause: the approval gate. The second form means there is no terminal (for example under Actions), so every gated call is declined.
Fix: answer y at the prompt. For unattended runs, use --verify build or --verify test to admit build and test commands.
blocked: command matches a disallowed pattern (%s)
Cause: the run_shell command screen. What it looks for is deliberately not published.
Fix: none; this is intended. The model sees the refusal and adapts.
path %q escapes the workspace / path %q is inside .git, which tools may not touch
Cause: the session's workspace confinement. This is intended.
verification tier %q needs the sandbox, … — model-written tests are never run unsandboxed; …
Fix: use --verify build, or run on a machine where the sandbox works.
unknown verification policy %q — use off, build, or test
Fix: correct --verify.
turn %d: %d consecutive malformed replies, giving up
Cause: the model returned three unparseable replies in a row. That is usually the wrong tier or an overloaded plane.
Fix: check --model (default coder), then tidde session resume .
refusing to navigate to non-local host %q …
Fix: pass --browser-allow-remote if you really mean it.
session %s: no console configured — report kept locally (set console_url in ~/.tidde.yaml, then `tidde session sync`)
Cause: --console-url has no default. Fix: set it and run tidde session sync.
session %s: report not delivered (kept pending for `tidde session sync`): %v
When %v is console 403: … with the body token does not carry the App's rights for org "…":
Cause: the console accepts reports only from tokens carrying the GitHub App's rights for its org.
Fix: sign in with tidde auth login through the same App, then run tidde session sync.
tidde session serve



Message
Fix




no repositories allowed — pass --repo for each repo a queued instruction may touch
pass --repo at least once; there is no wildcard


no console URL — set --console-url, TIDDE_CONSOLE_URL, or console_url in ~/.tidde.yaml
set the console URL


session commands require a personal GitHub App token (`tidde auth login`) for org %q — installation tokens are not accepted
run tidde auth login; CI tokens cannot queue or claim


could not resolve the GitHub login for this token; refusing to queue or claim a command without a verified identity
re-run tidde auth login --force


this console does not know its GitHub org: …
the console has no readable App installation and the GitHub organisation setting is unset; fix it on the console side


queue is full — drain it before adding more (HTTP 429)
let serve claim or finish the queued items first



Agents
The review, triage or self-heal comment says the model was unreachable
For example: the sovereign coder model was unreachable at …, or the coder model answered, but not in the review shape, so nothing from its answer is shown here.
Cause: a runtime model failure. It is posted as a degraded notice so a broken plane cannot look like "nothing found".
Fix: check the inference plane and the model router. Then re-comment @tidde_check or wait for the next sweep.
reviewer: INFERENCE_URL not set — … (same shape for every agent)
Cause: the workflow did not set the endpoint. This is a configuration failure, and it is loud by design.
The curator runs green every day but publishes nothing
Cause: the curator's dry-run switch is unset, which means dry.
Fix: set the Actions variable to the literal false.
### 🔒 Forger is DISARMED in the run summary
Fix: set the forger's arming switch, or arm forger in the console's agent controls.
A PR keeps its review:findings-open label
The label clears only on a clean review. Check for a pending draft from fixer/* or tidde-resolve/*, since the resolver does not re-attempt a PR with one. Otherwise wait for the resolver's three-hourly sweep. See Review Pipeline.
A dispatched review never finishes; core/review stays pending
A pending status older than 90 minutes is started again by the review sweep. Nobody needs to comment.
Console
PUT /api/agent-schedules/{name} returns nothing to change: send at least one of enabled, dryRun, schedule
Fix: include at least one of those fields. A 404 reading no scheduled agent named … means the name is not a scheduled agent.
GET /api/audit/verify answers 503
There is no persisted chain to check. The audit log could not be attached, and the chain is stderr-only for this process.
The session-admins list cannot be changed
PUT /api/session-admins refuses an empty list and one that removes the caller with nobody left. If it fails with not changed: the audit record could not be made durable first: …, the audit log is not writable.

docs/user-guide/overview-page/.title: Overview page
docs/user-guide/overview-page/.body:
The Overview page

Overview is the first page of the TIDDE console and the first row of its rail. It answers one
question: is anything wrong, and where do I go next? It is a summary: each line links to the
page that owns the subject.
What the Overview page shows

How a plan runs

You set a goal. TIDDE proposes a plan: the steps and which agent does each.
A reviewing model checks every step before it runs. A plan stops at the first step a guardrail
refuses, and a plan the judge dissented from cannot be approved.
A plan runs only once it is approved, by an agent admin or, when Autonomy
has armed unattended execution, within that policy.

running plan.

until a person plans or dismisses them.

A goal about code ends in a draft pull request. Merging, secrets and deletes stay with a person.
